sm: The host, Coffeezilla, says he is breaking his own rules against covering politicians and billionaires to investigate the president and his family's business dealings across crypto, meme coins, stablecoins and more. He notes that even some of the president's supporters now call this one of the most corrupt presidencies, and says he was threatened by a lawyer before publishing. He stresses that everyone named denies wrongdoing and that nothing is an accusation of crime. He recalls the Trump meme coin launching two days before inauguration, followed by a Melania coin, and cites Steve Bannon's strategy of flooding the zone. Researcher Molly White helped map the web, including the six hundred million dollars made from the Trump coin.

Molly White explains that the Melania coin lost about ninety nine percent of its value and the Trump coin about ninety five percent, so most buyers lost money, though top holders got a dinner with the president. The segment then turns to World Liberty Financial, a Trump family crypto project with a governance token and a stablecoin called USD1, which sold out five hundred fifty million dollars of tokens. Justin Sun invested seventy five million and later saw an SEC fraud case against him dismissed, before falling out with the company. The Wall Street Journal's Sam Kessler reports that four days before inauguration a UAE royal sheikh secretly agreed to pay five hundred million dollars for a forty nine percent stake. USD1 was then picked to close MGX's two billion dollar investment in Binance, and World Liberty says that choice was made on its merits.

The segment explains that the two billion dollars of USD1 reserves earns interest for the Trump family, while the UAE secured long-wanted advanced AI chip deals that were approved soon after. World Liberty denies any quid pro quo. Binance had its SEC case dropped and founder Changpeng Zhao was pardoned, which Trump said he did not know why beyond not knowing him, while Zhao said the pardon helped Binance return to the US. Binance also offered a twenty percent yield to customers holding USD1, and World Liberty says that is standard marketing. The host links this to the Genius Act, which Trump pushed, and to World Liberty's provisional bank charter approval, which the company says was done by career staff. He ends by introducing a one point five billion dollar deal with Alt Five Sigma.

The Alt Five Sigma deal reportedly paid five hundred million dollars to a Trump family entity and ninety million to the Witkoff family. Alt Five is run by the same people as World Liberty, and its stock fell about ninety four percent in a year. The segment notes Steve Witkoff, special envoy to the Middle East, has divested his stake, while Jared Kushner, an unofficial envoy, runs a fund that took two billion dollars from Saudi Arabia and sought five billion more. Isaac Saul discusses the four hundred million dollar Qatari plane, a nearly two billion dollar arms deal, a Qatar golf project worth five and a half billion, and later five billion dollars in military sales. The host then covers American Bitcoin, where Eric Trump and Don Jr. hold stakes after a deal with Hut Eight, whose CEO said the brothers brought capital market access and narrative.

The host lists the president's strategic Bitcoin reserve order alongside Trump Media's two and a half billion dollar Bitcoin reserve, with investor Don Wilson's SEC case dismissed weeks earlier, which Cumberland says is unconnected. He describes Trump posting about stocks he had bought, and Trump Media selling a real-time feed of market-moving posts for a hundred thousand dollars a month. He covers Crypto dot com's fifty million dollar purchase of Trump Media stock after its SEC probe closed, and exchanges donating to Trump causes after their cases were dropped. Trump Media also launched political index funds and agreed a six billion dollar stock merger with fusion company TAE. He notes most of these ventures have disappointed investors, with Trump Media posting about seven hundred twelve million dollars in losses.

Trump Media's Truth Predict prediction market flopped, but prediction markets are booming under CFTC chairman Mike Selig, and Donald Trump Jr. advises both Polymarket and Kalshi. Selig told Congress the agency plays no favorites, and Kalshi's CEO could not clearly explain Don Jr.'s role. Don Jr. is also a partner at 1789 Capital, which holds over a billion dollars in assets and invested in Vulcan Elements shortly before a government partnership was announced. ProPublica reported that the White House called to get that deal done, while the firm says it stays out of government dealings. The host also describes American Acquisition One, a three hundred million dollar SPAC advised by Don Jr. and Eric Trump, whose filing mentioned targeting companies that benefit from government contracts.

The host notes some language about preferential contracts was removed from the SPAC filing, then turns to Eric Trump advising robotics firm Foundation Future Industries, which has a twenty four million dollar Pentagon contract, though Wired said many contracts were older. He zooms out to the family's expansion into social media, crypto, prediction markets, fusion, Bitcoin, rare earths, SPACs and robots, all while the president oversees those industries. Disclosures show the president made about one point four billion dollars from crypto and two point two billion total. Forbes says Eric is ten times richer, Don Jr. six times richer, and Barron worth about one hundred fifty million dollars. He concludes that investors mostly lost money, and the episode ends with a comedic bar skit about a robot being thrown out.
